_aciklama: Blog yazısı çevirisi. Odak kelime: interface design principles / UI UX design service. Anahtar = kayıt numarası.
_degismeyenler: ETBİS kısaltması korunur + 'Türkiye's central e-commerce information system' açıklaması. Ticaret Bakanlığı → Ministry of Trade. Kişi adı İhsan Ar, marka adı TasarımMania. UI, UX kısaltmaları aynen.
_sozluk: arayüz tasarımı → interface design. görsel hiyerarşi → visual hierarchy. tutarlılık → consistency. geri bildirim → feedback. yakınlık ilkesi → proximity principle. erişilebilirlik → accessibility. bileşen kütüphanesi → component library. tipografi ölçeği → typographic scale. kontrast oranı → contrast ratio. boşluk basamağı → spacing step. beyaz alan → white space. punto → point size (18 punto → 18pt). dokunma alanı → touch target. mikro metin → microcopy. durum matrisi → state matrix. birincil eylem → primary action.
_devrik_cumle: Kaynak metin yer yer devrik cümle kullanıyor ('Yükselir hata oranı, …', 'Dağılır tıklama, …'). Türkçede üslup, İngilizcede bozuk sözdizimi olurdu; anlam korunup doğal sıraya çevrildi.

ceviri.14: User interface design is the arrangement of the visual elements on a screen according to the principles of hierarchy, consistency and feedback.
ceviri.16: A design system is the body of rules that governs colour, typography, spacing and components from a single source.
ceviri.34: Are interface design and user experience design the same thing?
ceviri.35: No. Interface design covers the visual layer on the screen, while user experience design covers the whole design of the interaction.
ceviri.36: What is the practical way to test visual hierarchy?
ceviri.37: Take a greyscale copy of the screen. If the primary action still stands out once the colour has gone, the hierarchy is working. If it doesn't, the size, weight and spacing settings need reworking.
ceviri.38: Is a component library necessary for small businesses too?
ceviri.39: Yes — in small teams the effect is greater still. A limited set of button, form and card definitions removes the burden of deciding from scratch on every new page. When designer and developer use the same names, delivery time shortens. On our projects, starting the library with fifteen components is usually enough. We widen it as the brand grows. The cost of opening a new page drops and the visual language doesn't drift. And because the decisions are gathered in one source, reviewing them gets easier too.
ceviri.41: It doesn't constrain it, it clarifies it. Rules on contrast, point size and touch targets are limits that simplify a design. When the limits are known, decisions take less time.
ceviri.42: How long does a UI UX design service project take?
ceviri.43: The length depends on the number of screens and the complexity of the components. On our projects, the design system and interface build for a corporate site of eight to ten screens is finished within a few weeks. On dashboard and app projects the number of states rises, so the schedule stretches. We settle the scope together in the first meeting.
ceviri.44: Is it possible to improve an existing interface without starting again?
ceviri.45: It is. On our own projects, corrections to hierarchy and feedback make a serious difference with limited intervention on the code side. We measure first, then draw up the order of priority.
ceviri.46: Do consistency and creativity conflict in design?
ceviri.47: They don't. The rules fix the basic components, while creativity stays free at the level of content and composition. A stable base is what makes bold decisions safe.
ceviri.48: Who should sign off on interface decisions?
ceviri.49: The authority to approve should sit with one person. Feedback from many directions at once is the fastest way to break consistency. We prioritise the comments we collect and carry them to a single decision-maker.

ceviri.60: Which Principles Does Interface Design Rest On?
ceviri.63: Which Principles Does Interface Design Rest On?
ceviri.64: Interface design is not a matter of taste about where each element on the screen ought to sit. There is a logic of decision behind it. Which button grows, which text shrinks, what the system says when the user does something — all of it rests on principles. When we build the digital surfaces of SMEs, we put those principles on the table. A UI UX design service is exactly that: this set of visual decisions, brought under discipline. Below we open up the logic behind the principles.
ceviri.65: Hierarchy separates the elements on a screen into layers by order of importance.
ceviri.67: What Are the Core Principles of Interface Design?
ceviri.68: Interface design rests on five core principles: visual hierarchy, consistency, feedback, proximity and accessibility. Those principles are the rule set that determines the size, the colour and the position of every element on the screen. Behind decisions that look like aesthetic preferences lies a measurable rationale. A team that knows the principles takes the argument out of the realm of taste.
ceviri.69: The principles are not independent of one another. If the hierarchy is weak, consistency is no use either; the user doesn't know where to look.
ceviri.70: In our UI UX design service
ceviri.71: each principle is scored on its own row. That way rounds of revision proceed against defined criteria rather than personal taste.
ceviri.73: The largest and darkest element on the screen is the user's first stop. Visual hierarchy is the principle of arrangement that separates elements by order of importance through size, colour and space. When the order of priority is clear, the user finds the main action in the first second. The difference between the heading, the supporting text and the button has to be sharp enough.
ceviri.75: A user who sees the same button in two different forms doesn't fully trust either of them. Consistency is the principle that ensures the same function is presented in the same visual language on every screen. Uniformity lowers the burden of learning; the pattern the user learns once is recognised on every page.
ceviri.76: What Does the Proximity Principle Do?
ceviri.77: Elements placed close together form a single group in the user's mind. The proximity principle clusters related areas with space and separates the unrelated ones. The form label sticks to its own field, the help text to its own line. When the spacing falls apart, which box a label belongs to becomes unclear and the error rate rises. That is why we set the spacing steps before reaching for lines or frames.
ceviri.78: How Does Visual Hierarchy Guide the User's Eye?
ceviri.79: The eye goes first to the largest and most contrasted element on the screen; hierarchy puts that reflex under the designer's control. If everything on the screen carries the same weight, nothing comes forward. The designer entrusts the primary action to a single element and lowers the tone of the secondary links. That separation is the visual counterpart of the decision.
ceviri.80: When we build the hierarchy we look at three settings: the typographic scale, the contrast ratio and the white space. In typography we follow the common scale convention and pick a ratio between 1.25 and 1.5; within that range the heading levels don't blur into one another. On contrast our own floor is clear: 4.5:1 on small text, 3:1 on text above 18pt. White space, meanwhile, does the grouping quietly.
ceviri.81: How Is the Focal Point Decided?
ceviri.82: In a UI UX design service we define a single primary action for every screen; the focal point is the strongest visual counterpart of that goal. Clicks scatter the moment a second button of equal weight is added. Simplicity here is a functional choice, not an aesthetic one.
ceviri.83: How Do We Audit the Hierarchy?
ceviri.84: The greyscale test takes the eye's judgement out of play. In a UI UX design service we strip out the colours and look at the screen again; if the order of priority is still visible, the structure is sound. If it isn't, the size and spacing get reset.
ceviri.85: Why Is Consistency the Backbone of Design Decisions?
ceviri.86: The user learns a pattern once; consistency is what keeps that pattern valid across every screen. The same action should sit in the same place, in the same form. When the pattern changes, the user has to learn it again. That burden pulls the error rate up. A component library is precisely what prevents it.
ceviri.87: We build consistency as a system, not a document. The rules on colour, typography, spacing and components are gathered in a single source. The number of businesses going digital in Türkiye is rising fast;
ceviri.89: — ETBİS is Türkiye's central e-commerce information system — the number of businesses trading online reached 634,611 in 2025. At that scale, the same interface pattern has to be repeated by different teams at different times. The error rate climbs whenever the same action sits somewhere different on every page.
ceviri.90: What Does a Component Library Solve?
ceviri.91: When a new page is opened the designer doesn't start from scratch, and the developer sees the same names. A component library is the structure that produces elements such as buttons, forms and cards from a single definition. Argument falls away and speed rises.
ceviri.92: How Do Brand Identity and Interface Language Meet?
ceviri.93: Brand colours are not used verbatim in an interface. We balance the corporate palette with neutral tones as the screen requires. Identity decisions and interface decisions are matched at the same table. A UI and UX design service is the work of translating a brand's language into the language of the screen.
ceviri.95: Feedback is the principle that the system gives a visible response to everything the user does. When a button is pressed the state should change; when a form is submitted the result should be readable. An interface that stays silent pushes the user into repeating the same action. Accessibility, in turn, guarantees that those responses can be perceived by everyone. This layer is not up for negotiation.
ceviri.96: Accessibility is the design approach that makes an interface usable for people with different visual, auditory and motor abilities. We test the colour-blindness scenario against every palette decision in the UI layer of the service. Information must never be carried by colour alone; an icon, a piece of text or a position has to give a second signal. As the age range of the users widens, decisions about touch targets and point size get stricter.
ceviri.97: How Fast Should the System's Response Be?
ceviri.98: When a user presses a button they should see the change at once; the system response is the interval between the action and the change in the interface. On operations that take longer, a progress indicator comes into play. An empty waiting screen is a reason to leave.
ceviri.99: How Should Error Messages Be Written?
ceviri.100: A red warning on its own isn't enough. An error message should state the problem and the solution in the same sentence, showing the user which field to correct and how. Within a UI UX design service, microcopy is part of the design too.
ceviri.101: “The number of businesses trading online, 600,800 in 2024, rose to 634,611 in 2025.”
ceviri.102: — Ministry of Trade, The Outlook for E-Commerce in Türkiye 2025
ceviri.103: How Do We Turn Interface Principles into Measurable Decisions?
ceviri.104: To turn the principles into measurable decisions, we score every screen against a fixed checklist. Hierarchy, consistency, feedback and accessibility each score out of five. A screen that doesn't collect at least four points under all four headings doesn't go live. That keeps the number of revision rounds predictable.
ceviri.105: The order we follow while running a UI UX design service is this:
ceviri.106: We draw up the screen inventory and write down the single primary action for each screen.
ceviri.107: We fix the typographic scale and the spacing steps at the very start.
ceviri.108: We build the component library and align the naming with the development team.
ceviri.109: We repeat the greyscale hierarchy test and the contrast audit on every screen.
ceviri.110: We design the feedback states (empty, loading, error, success) one by one.
ceviri.111: The Measures of a Design System
ceviri.112: The number of components, the number of colour variables and the number of spacing steps are all kept deliberately limited. A design system is, after all, the body of rules that governs interface decisions from a single source; the wider the limits, the weaker the consistency.

ceviri.115: Talk to Our Team About Interface Design
ceviri.116: A short initial assessment is enough to apply the interface principles to your own screens. We examine your existing interface under the headings of hierarchy, consistency and feedback. We give you the resulting picture in a plain report. After that we settle the scope together. The decision is yours, the measurement is ours. The first conversation commits you to nothing; it can be a new project or a screen you already have.
ceviri.117: We don't think of the UI UX side of a design service as separate from the commercial goal of the work. As the number of businesses refreshing their digital surface rises, the competition concentrates on the same screens. ceviri.151: Talk to Our Team About Interface Design
ceviri.152: Let's work out the road map that suits your scope together; let's settle the steps and the timing.
ceviri.155: In the hands of teams that know the principles, interface design stops being a guessing game. Hierarchy guides the eye, consistency lowers the burden of learning, feedback builds trust. When all three work at once, the screen explains itself. A well-run UI UX design service ties those three principles to documentation and to measurement. Let's see together which of them is coming up short on your screens.
